Practicable means able to be done — capable of actually being carried out in the real world, given the current situation, resources, and conditions. When you call something practicable, you are making one single claim: this can actually be done.

It is a test of feasibility. A plan, a solution, a method, or a course of action is practicable if it can realistically be put into practice. It is not practicable if it cannot.
The one distinction you must never confuse: practicable vs. practical

This is the most important thing to understand about this word, because these two words are neighbours that people constantly mix up — and mixing them up will cost you precision.

Practicable asks: Can it be done? (possibility)
Practical asks: Is it sensible or useful to do? (wisdom/utility)

Here is an example that makes this crystal clear:

Imagine you want to build a full-size bridge made entirely of solid gold.

Is it practicable? Yes. With enough gold and enough engineers, it can be done. The laws of physics do not forbid it.

Is it practical? Absolutely not. It would be absurdly expensive, wasteful, and pointless. Nobody with any sense would actually do it.

So the gold bridge is practicable but not practical.

Now flip it around. Suppose someone suggests you should fly to a meeting that is five minutes away by foot.

Is it practical? No — it's a silly waste of time and money for such a short distance.

Is it practicable? Yes — flying is a real, working technology, so it can be done.

The lesson: practicable is purely about whether something can be done. Practical is about whether it makes sense to do it.
A subtle but important nuance: "given the circumstances"

Practicable does not just mean "theoretically possible in some universe." It means possible here, now, given the constraints and conditions that actually exist. This is what separates it from a purely abstract "possible."

For example, a doctor working in a remote village with limited supplies might say, "We will do everything practicable to help the patient." That means: everything that can actually be done given what we have and where we are. It acknowledges real-world limits. This nuance is built right into the word — it lives in the practical, physical world, not in a vacuum.
Register: where and when this word is used

Practicable is a formal word. You will not hear it much in casual conversation — people in everyday speech tend to say "doable" or "possible" instead. However, you will encounter it frequently in:

  • Legal and official documents: "The notice must be given as soon as practicable." This is a very common legal phrasing, and it means: as soon as it can reasonably and realistically be done.
  • Policy, government, and regulations: "Authorities must take all practicable steps to ensure safety."
  • Engineering, planning, and business: "We need a practicable solution before the deadline."
  • Formal writing and reports: Anywhere precision matters and the writer needs to distinguish can be done from makes sense to do.
The most common phrases that use this word

Once you know these, you will recognize the word instantly in the wild.

"As soon as practicable" — This is perhaps the most common phrase. It means as soon as it can reasonably be done. It is softer than "immediately" because it acknowledges that real-world obstacles might exist. You will see this constantly in laws, contracts, and official notices.

"Reasonably practicable" — Used especially in health, safety, and legal contexts, this means: doable without imposing an unreasonable burden. The word "reasonably" reminds you that practicability is always measured against effort, cost, and circumstance.

"Wherever practicable" / "where practicable" — Meaning: in every situation where it can actually be done. For example, "Use renewable energy wherever practicable."

"A practicable solution / alternative / approach / measure" — Straightforward uses meaning: a solution (or alternative, etc.) that can actually be implemented in real conditions.

The antonym is impracticable, meaning not able to be done — impossible or unfeasible in practice. If a plan is impracticable, it simply cannot be carried out given real-world conditions. Do not confuse this with impractical either, for the same reason as above: impractical means unwise or not sensible, not impossible.
A final summary in one breath

Practicable = can actually be done, given real-world conditions. It says nothing about whether it is a good idea. It only asks whether it is achievable. It is a formal word most at home in legal, technical, and official writing, and its most dangerous neighbour is practical, which is about sense and usefulness — not feasibility.
